prompt: Find all integers $n$ for which $n^4+6n^3+11n^2+3n+31$ is a perfect square.

The planar diagram below, with equilateral triangles and regular hexagons, sides length 2 cm, is folded along the dashed edges of the polygons, to create a closed surface in three dimensional Euclidean space. Edges on the periphery of the planar diagram are identified (or glued) with precisely one other edge on the periphery in a natural way. Thus for example, $BA$ will be joined to $QP$ and $AC$ will be joined to $DC$. Find the volume of the three-dimensional region enclosed by the resulting surface.

solutions.title: Recognise a truncated tetrahedron
solutions.body:
The net consists of $4$ regular hexagons and $4$ equilateral triangles, all with side $2$ cm. After gluing, at every vertex one triangle and two hexagons meet (angle sum $60^\circ+120^\circ+120^\circ=300^\circ<360^\circ$), and each triangle is surrounded by three hexagons. This is exactly the surface of the **truncated tetrahedron**: take a regular tetrahedron of edge $6$ and cut off each of its four corners by a plane through the points one third of the way along the three edges at that corner. Each face of the big tetrahedron becomes a regular hexagon of side $2$, and each cut produces an equilateral triangle of side $2$; folding the given net reproduces this polyhedron (by Cauchy's/Alexandrov's uniqueness theorem the convex polyhedron with these faces and gluings is unique).

So the volume is that of a regular tetrahedron of edge $6$ minus four regular tetrahedra of edge $2$ (the cut-off corners).

A regular tetrahedron of edge $a$ has base area $\frac{\sqrt3}{4}a^2$ and height $a\sqrt{2/3}$, hence volume
$$V(a)=\frac13\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{4}a^2\cdot a\sqrt{\tfrac23}=\frac{\sqrt2}{12}a^3 .$$
Therefore
$$V=V(6)-4V(2)=\frac{\sqrt2}{12}\left(216-4\cdot 8\right)=\frac{184\sqrt2}{12}=\frac{46\sqrt2}{3}\approx 21.68\ \text{cm}^3 .$$

**Answer: $\dfrac{46\sqrt2}{3}$ cm³.**

solutions.title: Scaling check
solutions.body:
The truncated tetrahedron with edge $1$ is obtained from a tetrahedron of edge $3$ by cutting off four tetrahedra of edge $1$, so its volume is
$$\frac{\sqrt2}{12}(27-4)=\frac{23\sqrt2}{12}.$$
Volume scales with the cube of the edge; with edge $2$ we multiply by $2^3=8$:
$$8\cdot\frac{23\sqrt2}{12}=\frac{46\sqrt2}{3}\ \text{cm}^3 .$$

prompt:
Let $(a_i)_{1\le i\le 2015}$ be a sequence consisting of $2015$ integers, and let $(k_i)_{1\le i\le 2015}$ be a sequence of $2015$ positive integers (positive integer excludes $0$). Let
$$A=\begin{pmatrix} a_1^{k_1} & a_1^{k_2} & \cdots & a_1^{k_{2015}}\\ a_2^{k_1} & a_2^{k_2} & \cdots & a_2^{k_{2015}}\\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\ a_{2015}^{k_1} & a_{2015}^{k_2} & \cdots & a_{2015}^{k_{2015}}\end{pmatrix}.$$
Prove that $2015!$ divides $\det A$.
answer: $\det A$ is divisible by $a_1\cdots a_n\prod_{i<j}(a_j-a_i)$, the Vandermonde product of the $n+1$ integers $0,a_1,\dots,a_n$, and every Vandermonde product of $n+1$ integers is divisible by $0!\,1!\cdots n!$.

solutions.title: Vandermonde divisibility
solutions.body:
Write $n=2015$. We prove $n!\mid\det A$ for any integers $a_i$ and positive integers $k_j$.

**Step 1: pull out the $a_i$.** Since every $k_j\ge1$, row $i$ of $A$ is divisible by $a_i$, so
$$\det A=a_1a_2\cdots a_n\cdot\det B,\qquad B=\big(a_i^{e_j}\big),\ e_j=k_j-1\ge0 .$$

**Step 2: $\prod_{i<j}(a_j-a_i)$ divides $\det B$.** Consider the polynomial $D(x_1,\dots,x_n)=\det\big(x_i^{e_j}\big)\in\mathbb Z[x_1,\dots,x_n]$. Fix $i<j$ and view $D$ as a polynomial in $x_j$ with coefficients in $R=\mathbb Z[x_k:k\ne j]$. Dividing by the monic polynomial $x_j-x_i$ gives $D=(x_j-x_i)Q+R_0$ with $R_0\in R$. Substituting $x_j=x_i$ makes two rows of the determinant equal, so $0=R_0$. Thus $x_j-x_i\mid D$. The polynomials $x_j-x_i$ ($i<j$) are irreducible and pairwise non-associate in the unique factorisation domain $\mathbb Z[x_1,\dots,x_n]$, so their product divides $D$:
$$D=\prod_{i<j}(x_j-x_i)\cdot S(x),\qquad S\in\mathbb Z[x_1,\dots,x_n].$$
Evaluating at $x=a$ shows that $\det B$ is an integer multiple of $\prod_{i<j}(a_j-a_i)$.

**Step 3: rewrite as one Vandermonde product.** Put $b_0=0$ and $b_i=a_i$ for $1\le i\le n$. Then
$$a_1\cdots a_n\prod_{1\le i<j\le n}(a_j-a_i)=\prod_{0\le i<j\le n}(b_j-b_i)=:V(b),$$
and by Steps 1–2, $V(b)\mid\det A$.

**Step 4 (Lemma): for integers $b_0,\dots,b_n$, $\ \prod_{j=0}^{n} j!$ divides $V(b)$.** We have $V(b)=\det\big(b_i^{\,j}\big)_{0\le i,j\le n}$ (Vandermonde). The falling factorial $(x)_j=x(x-1)\cdots(x-j+1)$ equals $x^j$ plus an integer combination of $x^0,\dots,x^{j-1}$. Working from the last column down, add integer multiples of earlier columns to column $j$ to replace $b_i^{\,j}$ by $(b_i)_j$; this does not change the determinant:
$$V(b)=\det\big((b_i)_j\big)=\det\Big(j!\tbinom{b_i}{j}\Big)=\prod_{j=0}^n j!\cdot\det\Big(\tbinom{b_i}{j}\Big).$$
Each $\binom{b}{j}=\frac{(b)_j}{j!}$ is an integer for every integer $b$ (for $b\ge0$ it counts subsets; for $b<0$, $\binom{b}{j}=(-1)^j\binom{-b+j-1}{j}$). Hence $\prod_{j\le n} j!$ divides $V(b)$.

**Conclusion.** In particular $n!\mid V(b)\mid\det A$, i.e. $2015!\mid\det A$. (If some $a_i$ coincide or some $k_j$ coincide, $\det A=0$ and the claim is trivial anyway.) ∎

*Remark.* The official solution phrases Step 4 as an induction on $k$; the lemma above is the cleanest form of that argument and gives the much stronger divisibility by $1!\,2!\cdots 2015!$.

prompt: Consider the harmonic series $\displaystyle\sum_{n\ge1}\frac1n=1+\frac12+\frac13+\cdots$. Prove that every positive rational number can be obtained as an *unordered* partial sum of this series. (An unordered partial sum may skip some of the terms $\frac1k$.)
answer: Every positive rational is a finite sum of distinct unit fractions: take $1+\frac12+\dots+\frac1m$ as large as possible below $p$, then write the remainder ($<\frac1{m+1}$) greedily; the greedy step strictly decreases the numerator.

solutions.title: Greedy algorithm (Fibonacci–Sylvester)
solutions.body:
**Lemma.** Every rational $r$ with $0<r<1$ is a sum of finitely many distinct unit fractions $\frac1{m}$, all with $\frac1m\le r$.

*Proof by strong induction on the numerator $a$ in a representation $r=\frac ab$ ($a,b$ positive integers).* If $a=1$ we are done. Let $a\ge 2$ and let $n\ge2$ be the integer with
$$\frac1n\le r<\frac1{n-1},$$
i.e. $n$ is the least integer with $an\ge b$ (it exists, and $n\ge2$ because $r<1$). Then
$$r-\frac1n=\frac{an-b}{bn},\qquad 0\le an-b<a,$$
because $a(n-1)<b$. If $an-b=0$, then $r=\frac1n$. Otherwise $r'=r-\frac1n$ is a positive rational with numerator $an-b<a$ and
$$r'<\frac1{n-1}-\frac1n=\frac1{n(n-1)}\le\frac1n<1 .$$
By the induction hypothesis $r'$ is a sum of distinct unit fractions $\frac1m$, each $\le r'<\frac1n$, so each $m>n$. Adding $\frac1n$ gives a representation of $r$ by distinct unit fractions, all $\le r$. $\square$

**Main proof.** Let $p>0$ be rational and $s_m=\sum_{k=1}^m\frac1k$ ($s_0=0$). Since the harmonic series diverges, there is a unique $m\ge0$ with
$$s_m<p\le s_{m+1}.$$
If $p=s_{m+1}$ we are done. Otherwise $r=p-s_m$ satisfies $0<r<\frac1{m+1}\le1$. By the lemma, $r$ is a sum of distinct unit fractions $\frac1j$ with $\frac1j\le r<\frac1{m+1}$, i.e. $j>m+1$. These are distinct from $1,\frac12,\dots,\frac1m$, so
$$p=1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac1m+\sum\frac1j$$
is an unordered partial sum of the harmonic series. ∎

*Example.* For $p=\frac52$: $s_6=\frac{49}{20}<\frac52<s_7$, so $m=6$ and $r=\frac52-\frac{49}{20}=\frac1{20}$, giving $\frac52=1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac16+\frac1{20}$.

solutions.title: Write the integrand as an integral
solutions.body:
For $x>0$,
$$\arctan(\pi x)-\arctan x=\int_1^\pi\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\arctan(xy)\,dy=\int_1^\pi\frac{x}{1+x^2y^2}\,dy,$$
so the integrand equals $\displaystyle\int_1^\pi\frac{dy}{1+x^2y^2}$, a nonnegative function. By Tonelli's theorem we may swap the order of integration:
$$\int_0^\infty\!\!\int_1^\pi\frac{dy\,dx}{1+x^2y^2}=\int_1^\pi\left[\frac{\arctan(xy)}{y}\right]_{x=0}^{x=\infty}dy=\int_1^\pi\frac{\pi}{2y}\,dy=\frac{\pi\ln\pi}{2}.$$

(The official solution does the same on $[0,n]\times[1,\pi]$ and lets $n\to\infty$, using integration by parts to control $\int_1^\pi\frac{\arctan(ny)}{y}dy\to\frac\pi2\ln\pi$.)

**Answer: $\dfrac{\pi\ln\pi}{2}\approx1.798$.**

solutions.title: Frullani's trick
solutions.body:
Let $g(t)=\arctan t$. For $0<\varepsilon<R$, substitute $u=\pi x$ in the first part:
$$\int_\varepsilon^R\frac{g(\pi x)-g(x)}{x}dx=\int_{\pi\varepsilon}^{\pi R}\frac{g(u)}u du-\int_\varepsilon^R\frac{g(u)}u du=\int_R^{\pi R}\frac{g(u)}u du-\int_\varepsilon^{\pi\varepsilon}\frac{g(u)}u du .$$
On $[R,\pi R]$, $g(u)$ lies between $g(R)$ and $\frac\pi2$, so the first integral lies between $g(R)\ln\pi$ and $\frac\pi2\ln\pi$, and tends to $\frac\pi2\ln\pi$ as $R\to\infty$. On $[\varepsilon,\pi\varepsilon]$, $0\le g(u)\le g(\pi\varepsilon)$, so the second integral is at most $g(\pi\varepsilon)\ln\pi\to0$ as $\varepsilon\to0$. Hence the integral equals
$$\frac{\pi}{2}\ln\pi .$$

solutions.title: A tent function in word length
solutions.body:
**Answer: yes.**

Write $v_r=(a_r,b_r)$ and let
$$S=\{k_1v_1+\cdots+k_nv_n:\ k_i\in\mathbb Z\}$$
be the additive group they generate. For $p\in S$ define the *word length*
$$d(p)=\min\Big\{\sum_{i=1}^n|k_i|:\ p=\sum_i k_iv_i,\ k_i\in\mathbb Z\Big\}$$
(a minimum of nonnegative integers, so it exists), and set $d(p)=+\infty$ for $p\notin S$. Clearly $d(0,0)=0$.

**Key property.** For every $p\in\mathbb R^2$ and every $r$: $p\in S\iff p+v_r\in S$, and if $p\in S$ then $|d(p+v_r)-d(p)|\le1$. Indeed, if $p=\sum k_iv_i$ then $p+v_r=\sum k_iv_i+v_r$ has a representation of length at most $d(p)+1$, so $d(p+v_r)\le d(p)+1$; symmetrically $d(p)\le d(p+v_r)+1$.

Choose an integer $m>n/\varepsilon$ and define
$$f(p)=\max\Big(0,\ 1-\frac{d(p)}m\Big)\qquad(\text{so } f(p)=0 \text{ if } d(p)=\infty).$$

* (a) $f(0,0)=1-0=1$.
* (b) $f(p)\ne0$ only if $d(p)<m$, i.e. $p=\sum k_iv_i$ with $\sum|k_i|<m$. There are only finitely many such integer vectors $(k_1,\dots,k_n)$, hence finitely many such $p$.
* (c) The function $t\mapsto\max(0,1-t/m)$ is $\frac1m$-Lipschitz on $[0,\infty)$. If $p\notin S$ then $p+v_r\notin S$ and both values of $f$ are $0$. If $p\in S$ then $|f(p+v_r)-f(p)|\le\frac1m|d(p+v_r)-d(p)|\le\frac1m$. So for every $p$,
$$\sum_{r=1}^n|f(p+v_r)-f(p)|\le\frac nm<\varepsilon .$$

So such a function exists. ∎

(The official solution takes $m\ge n/\varepsilon$, which only gives $\le\varepsilon$; choosing $m>n/\varepsilon$ gives the required strict inequality.)

answer: $S$ is a discrete group, so $S=\mathbb Zs$ or $S=\mathbb Zs+\mathbb Zt$ with $s$ a shortest nonzero vector; take radius $R=\|s\|/2$ and centers $(2m+\tfrac12)s+nt$.

solutions.title: S is a lattice; pair up neighbours along the shortest vector
solutions.body:
**Step 1: $S$ is discrete.** Let $a$ be a positive common denominator of the rationals $\langle x_i,x_j\rangle$. By bilinearity $a\langle u,v\rangle\in\mathbb Z$ for all $u,v\in S$. Hence for $0\ne u\in S$, $a\|u\|^2$ is a positive integer, so $\|u\|\ge\delta:=1/\sqrt a$. Since $S$ is a group, distinct points of $S$ are at distance $\ge\delta$. Consequently every bounded set contains only finitely many points of $S$ (disjoint disks of radius $\delta/2$ around them fit in a slightly larger disk). So minima of $\|\cdot\|$ over nonempty subsets of $S$ are attained. As $x_1\ne0$, $S\ne\{0\}$; choose $s\in S\setminus\{0\}$ with $\|s\|$ minimal.

**Step 2: $S\cap\mathbb Rs=\mathbb Zs$.** If $u=cs\in S$, let $k=\lfloor c\rfloor$. Then $(c-k)s=u-ks\in S$ and $\|(c-k)s\|<\|s\|$, so by minimality $(c-k)s=0$, i.e. $c=k\in\mathbb Z$.

**Step 3: structure of $S$.** If $S\subseteq\mathbb Rs$, then $S=\mathbb Zs$ by Step 2. Otherwise choose $t\in S\setminus\mathbb Rs$ with $\|t\|$ minimal (possible by Step 1); $s,t$ are linearly independent and $\|s\|\le\|t\|$. We claim $S=\mathbb Zs+\mathbb Zt$. Let $u\in S$, write $u=ps+qt$ ($p,q\in\mathbb R$) and suppose $q\notin\mathbb Z$. Choose an integer $l$ with $c:=q-l\in[-\tfrac12,\tfrac12]$, $c\neq0$; then $v=u-lt=ps+ct\in S\setminus\mathbb Rs$. Let $h$ be the distance from $t$ to the line $\mathbb Rs$; then $h\le\|t\|$ and the distance from $v-ks$ to $\mathbb Rs$ is $|c|h\le h/2$ for every integer $k$. Choosing $k$ so that the component of $v-ks$ along $s$ has length at most $\|s\|/2$, we get
$$\|v-ks\|^2\le\frac{\|s\|^2}{4}+\frac{h^2}{4}\le\frac{\|t\|^2}{2}<\|t\|^2,$$
while $v-ks\in S\setminus\mathbb Rs$ — contradicting the choice of $t$. Hence $q\in\mathbb Z$, so $u-qt\in S\cap\mathbb Rs=\mathbb Zs$ and $u\in\mathbb Zs+\mathbb Zt$.

In the first case put $T=\{0\}$, in the second $T=\mathbb Zt$; in both cases $S=\{js+w: j\in\mathbb Z,\ w\in T\}$, and every nonzero element of $S$ has length $\ge\|s\|$.

**Step 4: the disks.** Let $R=\|s\|/2$ and, for $m\in\mathbb Z$, $w\in T$, let $D_{m,w}$ be the closed disk of radius $R$ with center $c_{m,w}=(2m+\tfrac12)s+w$. (There are countably many; list them as $D_1,D_2,\dots$.)

* $D_{m,w}$ contains $P_1=2ms+w$ and $P_2=(2m+1)s+w$, both at distance exactly $\|s\|/2$ from the center (they are diametrically opposite). If $X\in S$ is in the disk, then $\|X-P_1\|\le 2R=\|s\|$, with equality only if $X$ is the point opposite $P_1$, i.e. $X=P_2$. But if $X\ne P_1$, then $X-P_1\in S\setminus\{0\}$ has length $\ge\|s\|$. So $X\in\{P_1,P_2\}$: **(a)** holds.
* Every point $js+w$ of $S$ is $P_1$ or $P_2$ for $m=\lfloor j/2\rfloor$: **(b)** holds.
* Two distinct centers differ by $2(m-m')s+(w-w')$, a nonzero element of $S$, so they are at distance $\ge\|s\|=2R$. Two closed disks of radius $R$ whose centers are at distance $\ge2R$ meet in at most one point (none if $>2R$, only the midpoint if $=2R$): **(c)** holds. ∎

*Remark.* The construction even puts every point of $S$ in exactly one disk. The official solution's lattice step contains a slip (it claims $\|u-v\|\ge\|t\|$ for all distinct $u,v\in S$); Step 3 above replaces it by a correct argument.
